50321: Why one Bible produces many churches and what still unites them; how our assumptions about God and humanity flow all the way into how we live; three ways of handling Scripture (biblicist, liberal, and the Christ-centred contextual reading); and a step-by-step method that brings the whole course together.
50323: If there is one Truth and one Lord, why are there so many churches and doctrines? Who is right, and what actually unites us?
50324: Most Christian divisions grew from real history (language, politics, power and honest disagreement over hard texts), not from a Bible that says nothing clearly. The Truth is first a Person, Jesus (John 14:6); the churches agree on far more about him than they disagree on, and his prayer for unity (John 17) is grounded in our shared union with him, not in uniformity.
50326:
A doctrine is simply a teaching. The New Testament word is *didaskalia*, “teaching” or “instruction”. Paul tells Timothy to watch his life and his doctrine closely, because both matter (1 Tim 4:16). From the start, the church “continued steadfastly in the apostles’ doctrine” (Acts 2:42), meaning the shared teaching about Jesus that the apostles passed on.

Over time, Christians learned to sort teachings by weight. A *dogma* is a teaching a church regards as binding for all its members (for example, that God is Trinity). A *doctrine* may be held firmly by one tradition but not by another (for example, how baptism should be done). An *opinion* is a personal view that should never divide a church (for example, the exact order of end-time events). The American Baptist theologian Albert Mohler called this sorting “theological triage”, borrowing the word from emergency medicine: first-order issues define the faith, second-order issues usually shape which church you join, and third-order issues should never separate believers.

This lesson uses that simple idea throughout. Much confusion about “one Truth, so many denominations” disappears once we ask: which level of teaching are these churches actually divided over?
50328:
Division is not new. Paul and Barnabas parted ways over a person (Acts 15:36-40). Corinth split into fan clubs: “I am of Paul”, “I am of Apollos” (1 Cor 1:10-13). The early church fought over who Jesus is, and the great councils (Nicaea 325, Constantinople 381, Ephesus 431, Chalcedon 451) drew lines that still exist. After 451, the churches we now call Oriental Orthodox (Coptic, Ethiopian, Armenian, Syriac) did not accept the wording of Chalcedon, partly over theology and partly over language and politics.

In 1054 the Latin-speaking West and the Greek-speaking East exchanged excommunications. The issues included the authority of the bishop of Rome and the Western addition of the word *filioque* (“and the Son”) to the Nicene Creed, but centuries of language, culture and empire lay underneath. Those excommunications were formally lifted in 1965, though the churches remain separate.

The Western Reformation began in 1517. Lutherans and the Reformed (Zwingli, Calvin) both stressed the authority of Scripture and salvation by grace through faith, but disagreed about the Lord’s Supper. In 1525 in Zurich the first Anabaptists baptised adults who confessed faith, and many were persecuted by Catholics and Protestants alike. In 1534 the Church of England separated from Rome under Henry VIII, for political as much as theological reasons. Baptists emerged from English Separatists in 1609. Methodism began as a renewal movement inside the Church of England under John and Charles Wesley and became separate churches in America (1784) and Britain (after Wesley’s death in 1791). The Pentecostal movement grew from revivals at Topeka (1901) and Azusa Street, Los Angeles (1906). Since then thousands of independent, non-denominational and African, Asian and Latin American churches have formed.

Notice the pattern: some splits were about doctrine, but many were about language, nation, personality, or a renewal movement that its parent church could not hold.
50330:
Peter admitted that some things in Paul are “hard to understand” (2 Pet 3:16), and Paul said we now see “through a glass, darkly” (1 Cor 13:12). Sincere readers do disagree. The sociologist Christian Smith calls this “pervasive interpretive pluralism”: the same Bible, read by sincere and intelligent people, produces many different answers on many topics.

The deeper causes are the ones this course has studied. Different presuppositions (Lesson 10). Different views of how authority works: Scripture alone, or Scripture within the living tradition of the church (Lesson 9). Different handling of genre and literal language (Lesson 11). Different weight given to single verses (Lesson 14). Different starting points for the whole story: for example, whether God’s covenant with Israel and the church are one people or two (dispensational and covenant theology).

But it is also fair to say that interpretation is not the only cause. Pride, power, politics and fear have split churches over issues that Scripture itself treats as minor. Paul’s rebuke in Corinth was not “you read the text differently” but “you are acting like mere humans” (1 Cor 3:3-4).
50332:
A famous saying runs: “In essentials unity, in non-essentials liberty, in all things charity.” It is often credited to Augustine, but no one has found it in his writings. The earliest known source is a 1626 Latin peace tract by the Lutheran pastor Peter Meiderlin, who wrote under the pen name Rupertus Meldenius during the bitter quarrels that led into the Thirty Years’ War. Richard Baxter and others made it popular in English.

What counts as essential? Most churches point to the ancient creeds. The Apostles’ Creed (which grew from an early Roman baptismal creed), the Nicene Creed (325, expanded in 381) and the Definition of Chalcedon (451) summarise the core: one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit; Jesus truly God and truly human; his virgin birth, death, resurrection, ascension and return to judge; the forgiveness of sins and the life of the world to come. Paul himself passes on a short creed of “first importance”: Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose on the third day (1 Cor 15:3-4).

Around the year 434, Vincent of Lérins proposed a test for the core faith: what has been believed everywhere, always, and by all. Not every tradition draws the line in the same place. For Catholics and Orthodox, the sacraments and the church’s own teaching office belong much closer to the centre than most Protestants would place them. Honesty means admitting that even the list of “essentials” is partly disputed, while the creedal core is shared by the vast majority of Christians in the world.
50334:
On the night before he died, Jesus prayed for all future believers “that they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us: that the world may believe” (John 17:21). The model of this unity is the relationship of Father and Son, and its source is our being “in us”, that is, in God. It is unity by union, not by uniformity. Paul says the same: we are to keep the unity the Spirit has already made (Eph 4:3), because there is one body, one Spirit, one Lord, one faith, one baptism (Eph 4:4-6).

Christians disagree about what this unity should look like. Catholics teach that it is fully expressed in visible communion with the bishops in union with the bishop of Rome (Vatican II’s *Unitatis Redintegratio*, 1964, also calls other Christians “brothers” and “separated brethren”). The Orthodox see the one Church as the communion that has kept the apostolic faith and the Eucharist unbroken. Many Protestants speak of the “invisible church”: all true believers, wherever they worship. Pentecostals and charismatics often stress the shared experience of the Spirit across church lines.

The last century saw real movement: the World Council of Churches (1948), the Lausanne Movement (1974), and the 1999 Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification between Lutherans and Catholics, which said that the sixteenth-century condemnations on that topic no longer apply to the partner’s teaching as now presented.
50336:
If the Truth is first a Person (John 14:6), then unity is first a shared belonging to him. “No man can say that Jesus is the Lord, but by the Holy Ghost” (1 Cor 12:3). John’s test is confession of Jesus come in the flesh and love for one another (1 John 4:2; 1 John 4:7-8). Jesus said the world would recognise his disciples by their love (John 13:35), not by their uniform opinions.

This connects with the lens of this whole course. If Jesus is the centre, then the closer churches move to him, the closer they move to each other, like spokes moving toward the hub of a wheel. That picture does not erase real disagreements; it puts them in proportion. John Wesley put it simply in his sermon “Catholic Spirit”: even when we cannot think alike, we can love alike.

50474: Why does how I live depend on how I read? “Bad lifestyle comes from bad ecclesiology; bad ecclesiology from bad eschatology; bad eschatology from bad theology; bad theology from bad biblical interpretation; and bad biblical interpretation from bad presuppositions and anthropology.”
50475: What we assume about God and about what a human is flows downstream into how we read, what we believe, what we hope for, how we do church and finally how we live. The New Testament’s answer starts upstream: in Christ we learn who God is and who we are, and life flows from union with him, not from copying him from the outside.
50477:
The learner’s chain runs upstream like a river traced back to its source. *Lifestyle* is how we actually live. *Ecclesiology* is what we believe the church is and how it should work. *Eschatology* is what we believe about the end and the hope of the world. *Theology* (in the narrow sense) is what we believe God is like. *Biblical interpretation* is how we read the Bible. *Presuppositions* are the assumptions we bring before we read (Lesson 10), and *anthropology* is our view of what a human being is.

An example shows how it works. Suppose I assume that God is mainly an angry judge and that humans are worthless. I will read the Bible as a set of threats and rules. My theology will picture a distant God who must be kept happy. My eschatology will be about escape: the world will burn, so get out. My ecclesiology will make the church a holding room for the saved, or a fortress against the world. And my lifestyle will be marked by fear, withdrawal or control.

Jesus taught the same principle with a tree: a good tree bears good fruit (Matt 7:17-18). Fruit is the visible end of an invisible root. Paul prays that the eyes of our heart would be enlightened (Eph 1:18), because what we see shapes how we walk.
